title: Comparison and Limit Comparison Tests
trouble: Students compare in the wrong direction, showing a series is smaller than a divergent one.

blocks.html: Most series do not have a formula for their partial sums, and many have terms that are hard to integrate. But you know a lot of benchmark series: geometric series and the $p$-series from the The Integral Test and p-Series. Comparison tests let you borrow their behavior.

Suppose $0 \le a_n \le b_n$. The partial sums of $\sum a_n$ increase (the terms are not negative) and never exceed $\sum b_n$. If that is finite, they are bounded, so they converge (by the monotone convergence theorem). If instead $\sum a_n$ is infinite, the bigger $\sum b_n$ must be infinite too.
For the limit version: if $\frac{a_n}{b_n} \to L$ with $0 < L < \infty$, then eventually $\frac{L}{2}b_n < a_n < \frac{3L}{2}b_n$, so each series is trapped by a multiple of the other, and they behave the same way.

Direct comparison ($0 \le a_n \le b_n$): $\sum b_n$ converges $\Rightarrow$ $\sum a_n$ converges; $\sum a_n$ diverges $\Rightarrow$ $\sum b_n$ diverges. Limit comparison ($a_n, b_n > 0$): if $\frac{a_n}{b_n} \to L$ with $0 < L < \infty$, both converge or both diverge.

Conclusion
blocks.cap: Only two of the four comparisons tell you anything.

blocks.title: Direct comparison
steps: $\sum\frac{1}{n^{2}}$ converges ($p = 2$), so the smaller series converges.

blocks.title: Limit comparison
steps: For large $n$ the terms behave like $\frac{2n^{2}}{n^{4}} = \frac{2}{n^{2}}$, so compare with $b_n = \frac{1}{n^{2}}$.
$\sum\frac{1}{n^{2}}$ converges, so this series converges too.

blocks.html: Comparing in the wrong direction. "$\frac{1}{n + 1} < \frac{1}{n}$, and $\sum\frac{1}{n}$ diverges, so $\sum\frac{1}{n + 1}$ converges" is not valid: being smaller than a divergent series proves nothing (and in fact $\sum\frac{1}{n + 1}$ diverges). Before concluding, say the inequality out loud and check it against the table above. When the inequality goes the useless way, try limit comparison instead.

blocks.title: Picking the comparison
steps: The terms behave like $\frac{1}{3n}$. Limit comparison with $\frac{1}{n}$: $\frac{n}{3n - 1} \to \frac{1}{3}$.
(Direct comparison also works here: $\frac{1}{3n - 1} > \frac{1}{3n}$, which is bigger than a divergent series.)

blocks.name: seriespartial
blocks.cap: The partial sums of $\sum\frac{1}{3n - 1}$ keep growing, about like $\frac{1}{3}\ln N$: slow, but without bound, just like the harmonic series it was compared with.
